Fictional_Message: SMS: 'XYZ Bank Alert: Your KYC has expired and your account will be blocked today. Update now at [link removed] by entering your account number, debit card details and the OTP you receive. - XYZ Bank KYC Team'
Warning_Signs: 1) False urgency: says the account will be blocked 'today'; 2) Asks you to click a link in an SMS; 3) Asks for debit card details and an OTP by SMS; 4) Sent from a mobile number or sender you do not recognise
Safe_Response: Do not click the link, reply, or share any details. If you want to check your KYC status, visit your nearest bank branch or use your bank's official channels. If you suspect fraud, contact your bank only through official channels (the number printed on your bank card, passbook or statement, or the bank's official app or website address that you type yourself). You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: RBI's FAME booklet says banks never ask for account, card, PIN or OTP details through SMS, email or phone calls. Scammers create fear of losing access so that people act before thinking. An OTP should never be shared with anyone.
Official_Reference: RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 19 (Too good to be true) and Message 14 (Dos and Don'ts for Electronic Banking): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]; RBI Financial Education initiative: https://www.rbi.org.in/financialeducation/ [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026] [Note: the page lists the Financial Literacy Week 2026 theme 'KYC - Your First Step to Safe Banking']

Fictional_Message: Phone call: 'Hello, I am calling from the bank rewards team. You have earned Rs. 2,000 cashback. A 6-digit code has just been sent to your phone. Please read it out so I can credit the money to you.'
Warning_Signs: 1) Unexpected call offering free money; 2) Asks you to read out a code received on your phone; 3) Caller claims to be from the bank but you cannot verify this
Safe_Response: Do not share the code. End the call. Remember: never share an OTP with anyone, including someone who says they are bank staff. If you suspect fraud, contact your bank only through official channels (the number printed on your bank card, passbook or statement, or the bank's official app or website address that you type yourself). Report the number if you can. You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: An OTP is meant to approve an action on your own account, so giving it to another person can let them complete a transaction. RBI's FAME booklet advises never sharing OTPs with anyone, including bank staff.
Official_Reference: RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 2 (Deposit Accounts - good practices), Message 14 and Message 15 (Don'ts: never share OTP): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]

Fictional_Message: Chat message from an unknown person: 'Sorry, I sent Rs. 3,000 to you by mistake. I have sent a refund request on your UPI app. Please approve it and enter your UPI PIN so the money comes back to you fast.'
Warning_Signs: 1) Stranger says they paid you by mistake; 2) Asks you to 'approve' a request and enter your UPI PIN; 3) Pressure to act quickly; 4) You have not checked whether any money actually arrived
Safe_Response: Do not approve the request and never enter or share your UPI PIN. Decline or ignore the request. Check your bank SMS or app for any real credit. A UPI PIN is never needed simply to receive money. If you suspect fraud, contact your bank only through official channels (the number printed on your bank card, passbook or statement, or the bank's official app or website address that you type yourself). You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: A request that asks you to enter your UPI PIN is a payment request: it takes money out of your account, it does not bring money in. A UPI PIN is used to approve sending money and must never be shared with anyone.
Official_Reference: RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 13 (UPI Dos and Don'ts: review collect requests, never share PIN): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]; NPCI UPI FAQs - What is an UPI-PIN? and collect request answers: https://www.npci.org.in/what-we-do/upi/faqs [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026] [Needs further verification: the page says the UPI PIN authorises transactions and must not be shared, but the exact sentence 'PIN is not needed to receive money' was not found on this page; confirm with an NPCI or bank source before publishing]

Fictional_Message: Phone call: 'I am from XYZ Bank customer care. Your debit card will be blocked in 10 minutes because of suspicious activity. To stop this, please tell me your card number, expiry date, CVV and PIN.'
Warning_Signs: 1) Unrequested call creating panic; 2) Asks for card number, expiry date, CVV and PIN; 3) Short deadline of '10 minutes'
Safe_Response: Hang up. Do not give any card details, PIN or UPI PIN. Call your bank yourself using the number printed on your card, passbook or statement. If you suspect fraud, contact your bank only through official channels (the number printed on your bank card, passbook or statement, or the bank's official app or website address that you type yourself). You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: RBI's FAME booklet says not to share card details (card number, expiry date, CVV) or PIN with anyone. NPCI states that a bank's customer support will never ask for a UPI PIN.
Official_Reference: RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 15 (Don'ts: do not share card details and PIN) and Message 19: https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]; NPCI UPI FAQs - What is an UPI-PIN?: https://www.npci.org.in/what-we-do/upi/faqs [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]

Fictional_Message: SMS: 'Your parcel could not be delivered. Pay a small re-delivery fee of Rs. 29 at [link removed] and enter your card or UPI details, or the parcel will be returned.'
Warning_Signs: 1) Message about a parcel you may not be expecting; 2) Link from an unknown sender; 3) Asks you to type card or UPI details on a page opened from a message; 4) Uses a small fee and a deadline to make it feel harmless
Safe_Response: Do not click the link or enter any payment details. Delete the message. If you are expecting a parcel, check with the seller or courier using their official app or a website address you type yourself. If you suspect fraud, contact your bank only through official channels (the number printed on your bank card, passbook or statement, or the bank's official app or website address that you type yourself). You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: RBI's FAME booklet advises typing your bank's web address yourself, using secure (HTTPS) websites, and not entering or storing credentials on untrusted portals. Links in unexpected messages can lead to look-alike pages made to collect your details.
Official_Reference: RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 14 (Dos and Don'ts for Electronic Banking Transactions): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]

Fictional_Message: SMS: 'CONGRATULATIONS! You have won Rs. 25,00,000 in the Mega Festival Lucky Draw. To claim your prize, send your bank account details and pay a Rs. 4,500 processing fee to [unknown UPI ID].'
Warning_Signs: 1) You won a lottery you never entered; 2) Asks for your bank account details; 3) Asks you to pay money first to receive money; 4) Unknown sender and unknown payment ID
Safe_Response: Do not reply, pay, or share any account details. Delete the message. Talk to a trusted family member if unsure. If you suspect fraud, contact your bank only through official channels (the number printed on your bank card, passbook or statement, or the bank's official app or website address that you type yourself). You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: RBI's FAME booklet warns about fake lottery and prize messages and says RBI and banks never ask for account, card, PIN or OTP details by SMS, email or phone. If an offer sounds too good to be true, pause and think.
Official_Reference: RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 19 (Too good to be true?) and Message 18 (Sachet Portal): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]

Fictional_Message: Phone call: 'This is XYZ Bank technical support. Your account has a problem. Please install the screen-sharing app from [link removed] and tell me the code it shows so I can fix it for you.'
Warning_Signs: 1) Unrequested 'technical support' call; 2) Asks you to install an app from a link; 3) Asks for the code that gives them access to your phone screen; 4) Wants you to keep the call going while you open banking or payment apps
Safe_Response: Do not install the app or read out any code. End the call. If you already installed it, end the session, remove the app, and contact your bank immediately through official channels. Never share your UPI PIN, banking password or OTP. You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: Someone who can see or control your phone screen may be able to see messages, OTPs and anything you type. RBI's FAME booklet says never to share your mobile banking PIN, password or OTP with anyone.
Official_Reference: RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 14 (never share PIN, password, OTP) and Message 25 (avoid apps received as links over SMS/social media - written for digital lending apps): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal: https://cybercrime.gov.in/ and helpline 1930 [Partly verified: portal address and 1930 helpline confirmed through Government of India (MHA/PIB/Parliament) documents; direct page access was blocked, so re-check the live portal manually] [Needs further verification: no RBI/NPCI page specifically about remote-access apps was verified; add an official advisory on this topic before publishing]

Fictional_Message: Chat message from a 'buyer' of a handmade saree: 'I will pay Rs. 1,500. Scan this QR code to receive the money, then enter your UPI PIN to confirm.'
Warning_Signs: 1) Asks you to scan a QR code to 'receive' money; 2) Asks for your UPI PIN; 3) Buyer is in a hurry and wants you to follow steps exactly
Safe_Response: Do not scan the QR code or enter your PIN. To get paid, share your own UPI ID or show your own QR code, then check your bank SMS or app for the credit. Never share your UPI PIN. A UPI PIN is not required simply to receive money. If you suspect fraud, contact your bank only through official channels (the number printed on your bank card, passbook or statement, or the bank's official app or website address that you type yourself). You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: A payment QR code carries payee details (and sometimes an amount), and entering your UPI PIN approves a payment from your account. Receiving money does not need your PIN. Always read the payee name and amount on the screen before entering a PIN.
Official_Reference: NPCI UPI FAQs - QR based integration mode and UPI-PIN answers: https://www.npci.org.in/what-we-do/upi/faqs [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]; RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 13 (UPI Dos and Don'ts): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026] [Needs further verification: NPCI page describes what a QR code contains and that the PIN authorises payments; confirm the exact 'no PIN to receive' wording before publishing]

Fictional_Message: Video call: 'I am an officer from a government investigation team. Your Aadhaar number is linked to an illegal parcel. Stay on this call, do not tell anyone, and transfer Rs. 80,000 to a verification account to avoid arrest.'
Warning_Signs: 1) Threat of arrest; 2) Orders you to stay on the call and keep it secret; 3) Demands an immediate money transfer; 4) Contact came out of the blue and cannot be verified
Safe_Response: End the call and do not transfer money. Speak to a trusted family member or friend. Check the claim only by contacting the organisation through its official channels. If you suspect fraud, contact your bank only through official channels (the number printed on your bank card, passbook or statement, or the bank's official app or website address that you type yourself). You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: Scammers use fear and secrecy so that you cannot think calmly or ask for advice. Real banks do not ask for PIN or OTP by phone. Do not pay anyone because of a call or message that threatens you.
Official_Reference: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal: https://cybercrime.gov.in/ and helpline 1930 [Partly verified: portal address and 1930 helpline confirmed through Government of India (MHA/PIB/Parliament) documents; direct page access was blocked, so re-check the live portal manually]; RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 14 and Message 16 (notify your bank immediately of unauthorised transactions): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026] [Needs further verification: no verified official page on official-impersonation scams was reviewed; add one before publishing]

Fictional_Message: WhatsApp message from an unknown number: 'Hi, it's me, this is my new number. I am in trouble and my bank app is not working. Please send Rs. 20,000 right now to this UPI ID. I can't talk, don't call.'
Warning_Signs: 1) New number claiming to be someone you know; 2) Says 'don't call'; 3) Urgent request for a large amount; 4) Unfamiliar UPI ID
Safe_Response: Do not send money. Call the person on the number you already have saved, or ask another family member to confirm. Re-check the person and the payee before any transfer. Never share your UPI PIN. If you suspect fraud, contact your bank only through official channels (the number printed on your bank card, passbook or statement, or the bank's official app or website address that you type yourself). You can also report cyber fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930.
Explanation: RBI's FAME booklet advises not to transfer money without verifying the recipient first. NPCI notes that once a UPI payment is initiated it cannot be stopped, so checking before you pay is important.
Official_Reference: RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Fourth Edition, Feb 2024 - Message 13 (UPI Don'ts: verify the recipient before transferring): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/images/FAME202426022024.pdf [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]; NPCI UPI FAQs - stop payment answer: https://www.npci.org.in/what-we-do/upi/faqs [Verified: page opened 23-Nov-2026]
